text: Chapter 9 / 19 CFL conditions and domains of dependence Learning goal: Connect information speed to the reach of a stencil, and distinguish necessary from sufficient conditions. Advection transports information at finite speed. The grid points available to a numerical solution must cover the range from which physical information arrives. Otherwise, the discretization cannot approximate the correct dependence. This idea motivates the CFL condition. Covering the physical domain of dependence is different from preventing error amplification. In the appropriate setting, CFL is necessary; it is not a sufficient condition that stabilizes every difference scheme. Advection and the upwind direction For a>0, the exact advection solution is the initial waveform shifted to the right by a t. The upwind scheme uses the value to the left. For 0≤ν≤1, its new value is a convex combination of two old values. Reverse the direction when a<0. An example where CFL is not sufficient FTCS with centered spatial differences is unstable at ν=0.6 despite satisfying the domain-of-dependence requirement. Check amplification for the particular method. A large implicit stability region also does not restore temporal accuracy lost through coarse steps. Derive diffusion restrictions separately For the one-dimensional heat equation with centered space and forward Euler in time, r=κΔt/h²≤1/2. This explicit stability restriction follows from amplification factors or discrete eigenvalues. It is not obtained simply by reusing the finite-speed advection argument. A small worked example For upwind with ν=1.2, the coefficient 1-ν is negative. The figure compares this example with FTCS at ν=0.6. Both amplify, but their diagnoses differ. The first violates the upwind stability condition; the second satisfies the necessary CFL condition but uses an unsuitable scheme. A mode with a four-grid-spacing period makes amplification easy to measure. from math import sqrt nu = 1.2 print("upwind, theta=pi:", abs(1-2*nu)) nu = 0.6 print("FTCS, theta=pi/2:", sqrt(1+nu*nu)) Unstable controls are saved as diagnostics. A pass flag can mean that the intended instability was detected, so read the meaning of each criterion. Figure 9: Revisit the same amplification data through the necessity and sufficiency of CFL. Show answer Halve the time step. Question 2: What if the explicit diffusion ratio r is held fixed? Show answer The step scales with the square of grid spacing, so reduce it to one quarter. Common pitfalls Do not carry the one-dimensional coefficient 1/2 unchanged into multiple dimensions. Do not substitute implicit stability for temporal resolution of the model. Key points Distinguish advection and diffusion step restrictions. Check method-specific stability as well as CFL.
